title: Given coin denominations and a target amount, return the total number of distinct combinations that make up that amount (order does not matter). Coins may be reused.
shortTitle: Coin Change II — number of ways to make an amount

s1_definition.profdef: Unbounded-knapsack counting DP where dp[a] is the number of combinations that sum to amount a. We iterate coins in the OUTER loop and amounts in the INNER loop so each combination is counted once regardless of order, using dp[a] += dp[a−coin]. Base case dp[0]=1, time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).
s1_definition.analogy: A teller at National Bank of India wants to know how many different note combinations add up to a requested amount. For each denomination she adds in turn, she extends every smaller total by that note. Putting the coin loop outside stops her from counting "5 then 1" and "1 then 5" as two different ways.
s1_definition.oneliner: Coins outside, amounts inside, dp[a] += dp[a−coin], dp[0]=1 counts combinations not permutations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unbounded-knapsack counting DP where dp[a] is the number of combinations that sum to amount a. We iterate coins in the OUTER loop and amounts in the INNER loop so each combination is counted once regardless of order, using dp[a] += dp[a−coin]. Base case dp[0]=1, time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A teller at National Bank of India wants to know how many different note combinations add up to a requested amount. For each denomination she adds in turn, she extends every smaller total by that note. Putting the coin loop outside stops her from counting "5 then 1" and "1 then 5" as two different ways.

**One line to remember:** Coins outside, amounts inside, dp[a] += dp[a−coin], dp[0]=1 counts combinations not permutations.

sections.s2_technical:
Create dp of size amount+1, set dp[0] to one because there is exactly one way to make zero (take nothing), and leave the rest zero. Then loop over each coin on the outside and, for each coin, sweep amounts from the coin value up to target adding dp[a−coin]. For example: `for (int coin : coins) for (int a = coin; a <= amount; a++) dp[a] += dp[a - coin];`.

The order matters deeply. If amounts were outside and coins inside, you would count ordered sequences (permutations) and overcount. Coin-outer means each denomination is fully considered before moving on, so combinations are counted exactly once.

The time is O(amount · number of coins) and space is O(amount). A senior nuance is that this is the counting twin of the minimization Coin Change, and the loop order is the single most common bug: swapping the loops silently changes the answer from combinations to permutations.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a cash-planning tool must report how many distinct note combinations satisfy a withdrawal, so the ATM team can gauge flexibility. This is exactly how Coin Change II works.

Problem 2 — "5+1" and "1+5" are the same physical handful of notes and must not be double counted. This is exactly why the coin loop is the outer loop.

The mini-project builds a `CombinationCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input denominations are one, two, five with target five.

Step 1: dp[0] is one and every other entry starts at zero.

Step 2: After processing coin one, every amount has exactly one combination (all ones), so dp[5] is one.

Step 3: After processing coin two, dp[5] grows to count combinations using twos, reaching three.

Step 4: After processing coin five, dp[5] gains the single-five combination, reaching four.

Step 5: The final answers are four ways for five and zero ways for three using only twos.

```text
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — ATM Combination Planner (Coin Change II)
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] Amount 5 has 4 combinations
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] 5 with {1,2,5} → 4
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] Amount 3 has 0 combinations
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] 3 with {2} → 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  dp[0]=1, rest=0
    for coin in {1,2,5}:        ← coin OUTER = combinations
      for a=coin..5: dp[a] += dp[a-coin]
  after coin1: dp[5]=1 ; after coin2: dp[5]=3 ; after coin5: dp[5]=4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Coin Change II is a counting dynamic programming problem on the unbounded knapsack. I define dp of a as the number of distinct combinations that sum to amount a, I set dp of zero to one because there is exactly one way to make nothing, and I leave the rest at zero. Then for each coin I sweep amounts from the coin value up to the target and add dp of the amount minus the coin.

The single most important detail is the loop order. The coin loop must be on the outside and the amount loop on the inside, because that counts each combination exactly once. If I reversed them I would count ordered sequences, so five then one and one then five would be treated as two different ways, which overcounts.

In my project at National Bank of India, a cash-planning tool needed to report how many distinct note combinations could satisfy a withdrawal so the ATM team could gauge flexibility. I used this counting DP with the coin loop outside, and I always call out the loop order in interviews because swapping it is the classic silent bug that turns combinations into permutations.
